tagline: Horse country links timber fences, a topiary hunt and historic stables.
intro: The Horses and Hounds Scenic Byway crosses rolling Maryland countryside, linking horse farms, racecourses and historic estates. Maryland’s tourism office presents the byway as a drive through Hunt Country, where fox hunts and steeplechases remain popular and farms produce Thoroughbreds for major American tracks. Historic homes punctuate the rolling fields. The route’s equestrian connections extend from the timber fences of Worthington Valley to Ladew’s sculpted fox hunt and the preserved stable at Hampton.

One of its roads had an earlier agricultural purpose: Glen Arm Road formed part of Old Harford Road, carrying farm products from Maryland and southern Pennsylvania toward Baltimore’s port. The equestrian landscape also changed over time. The Maryland Hunt Cup began in 1894 as a contest between two hunt clubs, moving among locations before acquiring a permanent home in Worthington Valley in 1922.

Start westward from Cockeysville on Shawan Road, then cross Worthington Valley on Tufton Avenue before heading toward Glyndon and Butler. Continue through Upperco, Hereford and Monkton; the longer eastern branch enters Harford County and passes Ladew Topiary Gardens on its return. Southward, the route reaches Loch Raven Reservoir and Glen Arm, with a side route ending at Hampton National Historic Site near Towson.

moments.title: Worthington Valley
moments.text: Four miles and 22 timber fences define the Maryland Hunt Cup, whose permanent home is Worthington Valley. The race began in 1894 to compare the hunting horses of the Elkridge and Green Spring clubs. Eligibility widened from those two clubs to Maryland clubs, then to clubs throughout North America in 1903. Worthington Valley became the permanent venue in 1922, after the race had moved among several locations during its early years. The event remains limited to amateur jockeys. Its solid timber fences imitate the hunt country where many competitors train, bringing that working landscape into the racecourse itself.

moments.title: Ladew Topiary Gardens
moments.text: At Ladew, a fox hunt takes the form of clipped plants: horses, riders, dogs and foxes clear a hedge. Harvey S. Ladew bought a farm in 1929 and established the gardens in the 1930s. His travels in England, where he hunted frequently, strongly influenced the topiary. The grounds divide into 15 garden rooms devoted to individual colors, plants or themes. Two crossing axes meet at an oval swimming pool, giving the separate rooms an organizing framework. House and gardens opened to the public in 1971. Other clipped figures include swans, a giraffe and a Chinese junk complete with sails, extending Ladew’s subjects beyond the hunt.
moments.notice: Look for the fox hunt shaped from topiary, with riders, horses, dogs and foxes clearing a hedge.

moments.title: Hampton National Historic Site
moments.text: Hampton’s 1805 stable connects the Ridgely family’s racing interests to the work of free and enslaved Black jockeys and grooms. The Elkridge Hunt Club met at the estate, and the Maryland Hunt Cup ran through its fields. Under Charles Carnan Ridgely, more than 300 enslaved people worked the fields and household of an estate that also included ironworks, mills and quarries. The preserved estate includes the Georgian mansion, gardens and original stone quarters where enslaved people lived. Those quarters contain exhibits on enslaved life at Hampton; the stone used to build them came from the Ridgelys’ quarry.
